entry.title: The minds behind Matryoshka
entry.content:
Nathan Godey

Nathan Godey is a researcher in natural language processing and machine learning whose work focuses on language modeling, model representations, and training efficiency. His research explores how language models learn and how their architectures and training methods can be improved.

Matryoshka Language Model Suites fits closely into this research profile. The paper investigates how models of different sizes can be trained within a shared architecture, reducing training costs while maintaining performance. This extends his broader interest in developing more efficient and effective language models.

Yoav Artzi

Yoav Artzi is a computer scientist and researcher in natural language processing and machine learning. His research has covered language understanding and generation, interactive language systems, and methods for training models to perform complex language tasks.

Matryoshka Language Model Suites fits into his broader research through its focus on improving language model training and deployment. Although the paper is more concerned with model architecture and computational efficiency than with interactive systems or language understanding, it aligns with his wider interest in advancing language modeling methods and making them more effective in practice.
entry.summary: The paper closely aligns with Nathan Godey’s research on efficient language model design and complements Yoav Artzi’s broader work on advancing language modeling methods.

entry.title: A new way of speculative decoding and on policy distillation

link.title: A new way of speculative decoding and on policy distillation

entry.content:
The Teacher Is a Direction, Not a Destination: Extrapolating RL-Induced Representation Residuals in On-Policy Distillation (Hao Li, MeiJia Chen, Weijie Ren, Donghan Li, Zijun Tian, Jingchun Huang, Naibo Wang) this paper introduce a new method to on policy distillation called RIDE, that try to make the student model surpass the teacher rather to simply imitate it.

WaveFront Decoding: Parallelized Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models (Hyeongju Ha, Jae-Joon Kim) this paper introduce a new way for speculative decoding for looped language models, that parallelizes token drafting and verification across different recurrence depths, significantly accelerating inference without requiring an additional draft model.
entry.summary: 2 papers that expand on ideas used in the matryoshka suits paper.

entry.title: A better Figure 2
entry.content:
The original

Figure 2 explores how to distribute 39 Transformer layers among three nested model blocks (500M, 1.5B, and 3B parameters). Each point represents a possible layer allocation $(n_1,n_2,n_3)$, where $n_1+n_2+n_3=39$.

The authors use two ternary plots: one showing KV-cache memory per token, and another showing theoretical inference FLOPs per token. Their goal is to choose an architecture with approximately the same memory and computational requirements as a conventional 3B model: 266 KB/token and 5.54 GFLOPs/token.

The authors select the configuration $(24,10,5)$, marked by a gold star.

The problem is that the key result is a tradeoff between two resources, but the visualization separates them into two different plots. Readers must understand ternary coordinates, locate the same configuration in both panels, interpret two color scales, and mentally combine the results.

This makes it difficult to answer the central question: Which architectures achieve a good balance between memory and computation, and why was this particular configuration selected?

The redesign

I suggest replacing the two ternary plots with a single 2D scatter plot, where each point represents one feasible architecture:

  • X-axis: KV-cache memory (KB/token).
  • Y-axis: Theoretical inference computation (GFLOPs/token).
  • Dashed reference lines: The Vanilla 3B model’s memory and FLOPs.
  • Highlighted star: The selected configuration $(24,10,5)$.
  • Tooltips: The layer allocation $(n_1,n_2,n_3)$ and resource requirements of each architecture.

The intersection of the two dashed lines represents the Vanilla baseline. Points near this intersection have similar memory and computational requirements, while points to the bottom-left use fewer resources on both axes.

The following Chart.js implementation establishes the reference axes using the paper’s reported values. The complete redesign would add the feasible architectures from Figure 2, reconstructed using the formulas in Appendix B.

{
  "type": "scatter",
  "data": {
    "datasets": [
      {
        "label": "Vanilla 3B baseline",
        "data": [{"x": 266, "y": 5.54}],
        "backgroundColor": "#222222",
        "borderColor": "#222222",
        "pointRadius": 8,
        "pointStyle": "crossRot"
      },
      {
        "label": "Vanilla KV-cache reference",
        "data": [
          {"x": 266, "y": 5.05},
          {"x": 266, "y": 6.05}
        ],
        "showLine": true,
        "borderColor": "#888888",
        "borderDash": [6, 5],
        "borderWidth": 1.5,
        "pointRadius": 0
      },
      {
        "label": "Vanilla FLOPs reference",
        "data": [
          {"x": 175, "y": 5.54},
          {"x": 355, "y": 5.54}
        ],
        "showLine": true,
        "borderColor": "#888888",
        "borderDash": [6, 5],
        "borderWidth": 1.5,
        "pointRadius": 0
      }
    ]
  },
  "options": {
    "responsive": true,
    "plugins": {
      "title": {
        "display": true,
        "text": "Finding the right architecture: KV cache vs. inference FLOPs"
      },
      "subtitle": {
        "display": true,
        "text": "Baseline reference; feasible architecture points to be added"
      },
      "legend": {
        "position": "bottom"
      }
    },
    "scales": {
      "x": {
        "type": "linear",
        "min": 175,
        "max": 355,
        "title": {
          "display": true,
          "text": "KV cache (KB per token)"
        }
      },
      "y": {
        "min": 5.05,
        "max": 6.05,
        "title": {
          "display": true,
          "text": "Theoretical inference FLOPs per token (G)"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

In the completed visualization, all feasible configurations would appear as small, semi-transparent points, with the selected configuration highlighted by a gold star. Hovering over a point would reveal its exact layer allocation and corresponding resource costs.

What the new figure shows that the old one didn’t

  • The tradeoff becomes immediately visible. Instead of mentally combining two ternary plots, readers can directly observe the relationship between memory requirements and computational cost. Architectures that save memory at the expense of computation, or vice versa, become easy to identify.
  • The baseline becomes a meaningful reference point. The intersection of the dashed lines represents the conventional 3B model. Readers can immediately see which architectures are more or less expensive on either dimension.
  • The architectural choice becomes easier to justify. The selected $(24,10,5)$ configuration can be highlighted relative to the baseline, clearly demonstrating how closely it matches both resource requirements.
  • Better configurations become easier to identify. The new plot makes it easy to see which architectures use less memory and computation, and which require a tradeoff between the two.

Design decisions

  • One scatter plot instead of two ternary plots, because the central question is about balancing two resource metrics rather than visualizing the proportions of three layer groups.
  • Direct comparison with Vanilla, using reference lines at 266 KB/token and 5.54 GFLOPs/token instead of separate color scales.
  • Highlight the selected configuration, making the authors’ final architectural decision easy to identify.
  • Interactive tooltips for layer allocations, preserving the architectural information encoded by ternary coordinates without requiring readers to interpret three axes.

The original ternary plots are still valuable for understanding how changing the relative depths affects memory and computation. They could remain in the appendix for readers interested in the architectural search space.

Interestingly, Appendix C (Figure 9) already uses a similar FLOPs-versus-KV-cache scatter plot to compare total layer budgets of 28, 39, and 50. My proposal is to apply that more intuitive representation to the within-39-layer allocation search in Figure 2, where it would directly support the selection of the final architecture.

Data: Figure 2, Table 1, and Appendices B–D of Matryoshka Language Model Suites (Godey and Artzi, 2026), arXiv:2608.09703.
entry.summary: Figure 2 uses two ternary plots to select a model architecture, but the key tradeoff between memory and computation is hidden across separate panels

entry.title: Rewriting the abstract
entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract is concise and clear, but readers unfamiliar with language model suites may not understand why they are important. The abstract should briefly explain the motivation for developing suites of models at different scales, so that readers can appreciate not only the contribution of this paper to the field, but also the broader significance of the problem it addresses.

Before and after

Before Training a language model suite classically requires training each model separately and serving them independently. We improve both training and inference efficiency by stacking sub-models of increasing size into a single nested architecture trained end-to-end. This Matryoshka training framework reduces the total parameter count of the suite, enables low-cost distillation from the largest to all smaller sub-models at every training step, and is well-suited for speculative decoding as the draft model is contained within the verifier. We validate our approach by training a Matryoshka suite comprising 500M, 1.5B, and 3B sub-models. Our suite is on par with independently trained baselines on benchmark performance and validation and out-of-domain perplexities, while using 36% less training compute and improving the throughput of speculative decoding by 14–26%. We also ablate key architectural choices, offering guidance for building strong Matryoshka LM suites.
After Language model suites provide models at different scales to accommodate diverse computational and memory constraints, allowing users to choose models suited to their deployment requirements. Training a language model suite classically requires training each model separately and serving them independently. We improve both training and inference efficiency by stacking sub-models of increasing size into a single nested architecture trained end-to-end. This Matryoshka training framework reduces the total parameter count of the suite, enables low-cost distillation from the largest to all smaller sub-models at every training step, and is well-suited for speculative decoding as the draft model is contained within the verifier. We validate our approach by training a Matryoshka suite comprising 500M, 1.5B, and 3B sub-models. Our suite is on par with independently trained baselines on benchmark performance and validation and out-of-domain perplexities, while using 36% less training compute and improving the throughput of speculative decoding by 14–26%. We also ablate key architectural choices, offering guidance for building strong Matryoshka LM suites.

The general rule

Briefly explain why the problem your paper addresses matters, so readers understand the broader motivation before encountering the technical contribution.
entry.summary: Why should we care about language model suites ?

entry.title: What Makes a Chain of Thought Easy to Learn?

link.title: What Makes a Chain of Thought Easy to Learn?

entry.content:
In Matryoshka Language Model Suites, the authors use Knowledge Distillation (KD) to train smaller models using the predictions of a larger model.

This is a good opportunity to explore a related topic: learning from Chain-of-Thought (CoT). In particular, we’ll discuss how Knowledge Distillation can be used to transfer reasoning abilities from large language models to smaller ones, and what makes this approach effective.

But first, let’s introduce Chain-of-Thought reasoning.

From Answers to Reasoning

One of the important developments in LLMs is Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning: instead of producing an answer directly, a model generates intermediate reasoning steps before arriving at its final answer.

For example, consider a simple multiplication problem:

Question: What is 17 × 24?

Answer only: 408.

With CoT: 17 × 24 = 17 × (20 + 4) = 340 + 68 = 408.

CoT can improve a model’s ability to solve multi-step reasoning problems at inference time. But it can also play an important role during training, by providing supervision on the intermediate reasoning steps rather than only the final answer.

Knowledge Distillation: Learning from a Teacher Model

Traditionally, language models were trained primarily on human-generated text. Today, model-generated synthetic data has become an important ingredient in LLM training, particularly during post-training.

One way to leverage stronger models is through Knowledge Distillation, where a smaller student model learns from a larger teacher model.

For autoregressive LLMs, the teacher can generate training sequences

\((y_1,\ldots,y_T),\) potentially including Chain-of-Thought reasoning. One way to train the student is to minimize the following distillation loss, which encourages it to match the teacher’s next-token probability distribution:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left( p_{\mathrm{teacher}}(\cdot \mid x,y_{<t}) \,\|\, p_{\mathrm{student}}(\cdot \mid x,y_{<t}) \right).\]

Here, $x$ is the question, $y_{<t}$ contains the preceding tokens, $p$ gives next-token probabilities, and $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ (Kullback Leibler divergence) measures how much the teacher’s and student’s distributions differ.

Does distilling reasoning actually help?

In Distilling Step-by-Step (Hsieh et al., 2023), the authors show that teacher-generated rationales can substantially improve data efficiency. In one experiment, a 770M-parameter student outperformed a few-shot prompted 540B-parameter teacher on a reasoning benchmark.

DeepSeek-R1 (2025) provides another prominent example: reasoning traces generated by a powerful model were used to train smaller models, leading to strong reasoning performance.

These examples use supervision on generated reasoning tokens, rather than necessarily matching the teacher’s full probability distributions as in the equation above. Both approaches transfer information from the teacher to the student.

In my view, one way to understand the benefit of distillation is that it gives the student a richer learning signal: reasoning traces expose intermediate steps, while teacher probabilities provide information beyond the selected tokens. This suggests that we should ask not only whether a CoT is correct, but also how useful the information it provides is for learning.

How Does CoT Help Simple Student Models Learn?

One possible explanation is that CoT makes difficult learning problems easier by exposing intermediate computations.

Suppose the target function is a composition of several operations:

\[y = f_3(f_2(f_1(x))).\]

In ordinary supervised learning, the student only observes input-output pairs $(x,y)$.

It must learn the entire computation from these examples.

With complete CoT supervision, the student also observes the intermediate values:

\[z_1=f_1(x), \quad z_2=f_2(z_1), \quad y=f_3(z_2).\]

Instead of learning the entire mapping directly, the student can learn to generate a sequence of simpler intermediate computations.

Of course, additional supervision does not guarantee easier learning in every setting. But it suggests that the structure of the reasoning trace can fundamentally change the learning problem.

In our recent theoretical work, we investigate an idealized version of this phenomenon. We show that carefully structured CoT can help even a single autoregressive neuron learn complex computations, including tasks performed by much larger neural networks or any polynomial-time Turing machine. The key is to provide the intermediate steps during training. Without those steps, learning from questions and final answers alone can be provably hard.

This suggests that a good CoT should be judged not only by whether it reaches the correct answer, but also by how easily the student can learn from it. A longer trace with simple steps might be more useful than a shorter one with difficult jumps. The goal, then, is to design reasoning traces that make learning easier for the particular student.
entry.summary: How teacher-generated reasoning can help smaller models learn, and why the structure of a reasoning trace might matter.

entry.title: How autoregressive and diffusion LMs imitate each other, and why it is inefficient

link.title: How autoregressive and diffusion LMs imitate each other, and why it is inefficient

entry.content:
Why this matters

In week 1 it was claimed that diffusion and autoregressive models are equivalent: each can reach the same results as the other, only at a higher cost. To make the claim easier to follow, here is a simple illustration.

The idea

Both model types do one thing: they assign a probability to every possible sentence. The difference is only in how they produce a sentence from that distribution.

What is going on. An autoregressive model is a function that answers one question: given the words so far, what comes next? A masked diffusion model answers a different one: given a sentence with holes, what goes in each hole? Both learned from the same text, so both know the same facts, for example how often “It’s raining outside today” occurs. They only take the question in a different shape.

Why this is always possible, not just in the example. Any distribution over sequences can be written as a product of “next given previous” terms. That is the chain rule of probability, not a property of neural networks. So whatever distribution a diffusion model produces, an autoregressive factorization of it exists, and a large enough autoregressive model can learn it. The other direction is easier: a masked diffusion model that unmasks exactly one position per round, left to right, is an autoregressive model. Autoregression is a special case of diffusion with a fixed unmasking order.

So what is the difference? The cost. Since the model is just a function and the generation loop around it is ordinary code, imitating the other model means writing a different loop around the same weights, and the price is the number of calls. To get what diffusion gets in one call, a table of candidates for every position, the autoregressive loop has to ask about every possible beginning: 3 calls for position 2, 9 for position 3, 27 for position 4. In our tiny world that is 44 calls instead of 2; with a real vocabulary it is not feasible. The other direction is cheaper but still wasteful: diffusion commits one position per call, left to right, computing all positions every time and discarding most of them. Four calls instead of two, and its parallelism is gone. This is the “you wouldn’t run it in polynomial time, you’d use the other one” remark from class.

One caveat. The equivalence is about ideal models with enough capacity and enough steps. Real models learn differently from the same data: autoregressive models train on correct text and then have to continue their own mistakes; parallel generation has the multimodality problem (each position picks something locally plausible, and together they do not fit). “What is possible” and “what actually happens” are two different levels, and the distinction comes up everywhere in this field.

Why it matters for the course. Most of the papers we will read are about autoregressive models, because that is what most research uses. The equivalence is the reason this is fine: what we learn about how one kind of model learns, remembers and fails carries over to the other. The architecture sets the cost, not what can be learned.
entry.summary: A claim from week 1, made easier to follow with pictures: each model type can do what the other does, and what it costs to do so.

entry.title: Critique of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

link.title: Critique of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

entry.content:
Summary of the claims

  1. Matryoshka architecture saves compute in training, including distillation
  2. Matryoshka architecture saves compute in inference through better draft for speculative decoding
  3. Matryoshka architecture gets comparable results for the large model and the sub models as the classic methods
  4. Ablations - the different components are actually needed (inter-model junction normalization, width/depth of submodels)

Strengths

  1. Simple architecture “trick” that achieves on-par results with great efficiency wins.
  2. Comparisons to the vanilla suite - including both FLOP-equivalent and token-equivalent variations.
  3. Ablations study.
  4. Stated novelty compared to MatFormer.

Weaknesses

  1. 35B tokens for training a 3B parameter model is not always a good enough data point for comparison. Considering chinchilla as the baseline, I’d expect about 60B tokens.
  2. The high acceptance rate is just an artifact of the distillation. I understand the distillation here is cheaper, but comparing a teacher-student acceptance rate and two independent models acceptance rate is less surprising than it initially sounds. Appendix A Figure 8 - shows the effect of alpha_d=0, which is one way to test it, but the other way (comparing to vanilla + distillation) is more interesting I think (and also here the results are not that conclusive).
    • The other throughput gains come from the stated memory benefits.
    • Also, it seems that the speculative decoding wasn’t compared to the best speculative decoding that can be done on the vanilla suite - e.g. smaller vanilla draft.
  3. The paper assumes each model in a model suite is trained independently, I’m not sure that’s the case - it depends on whether in some cases, seeing synthetic high quality training data produced by the largest model might be more efficient in training than seeing the full raw data. In that case the assumed compute savings in training will be lower.
  4. The paper uses the same hyperparameters for training the matryoshka-suite and the vanilla-suite. There’s no reason to assume that the optimal hyperparameters will be the same. Did the the hyper parameters here were chosen to optimize the matryoshka-suite training?
  5. I can think of more ways to implement the inter-model junction (even just a learned projection), and the ablation only treated the normalization and not the major choice of how to implement the inter-model junction itself (concat output and new embedding)
  6. It seems all of the experiments were only executed once - No mention of repetition, and no error bars.
  7. The paper implies an advantage that can be used in real world scenarios. In order for this claim to hold, the “open question” regarding post training becomes a critical question that should be addressed here.
  8. The expected benefit in train efficiency is dependent on the proportions between the model sizes, so for a model suite that grows “faster” than the tested suite we will get lower efficiency boosts.

How it could have been improved

  1. Scale up and down - how does scale affect the results? Parameters & Tokens
  2. Compare the speculative decoding to a distilled suite, and to better speculative decoding configurations.
  3. I couldn’t think of an idea how to treat the option of creating high quality synthetic data, because it is extremely dependent on implementation details. Maybe a way to treat it is to use the “prune and distill” pardigm.
  4. Optimize the hyper-parameters for the vanilla suite and for the matryoshka suite seperately.
  5. More ablations - specifically in the inter-model junction.
  6. Statistical certainty.
  7. Address the post-training question.

Verdict

The idea is clean and has some novelty over previous methods. I would accept with some required improvements:

  1. Speculative decoding baseline
  2. Statistical Certainty (Even though I’m aware it’s on a compute budget)
  3. Address the scale and the specific configuration (ratio between model sizes).
entry.summary: Clean idea to boost efficency for training model suites, should use more extensive experiments

entry.title: Visualizing the core idea of Matryoshka LM Suites

link.title: Visualizing the core idea of Matryoshka LM Suites

entry.content:
Core idea:

The core idea of the paper (Godey and Artzi, 2026) is explained in Section 2 and in Figure 1(a). A model suite is a group of models of different sizes, here 500M, 1.5B and 3B parameters. Usually, each model is trained separately. The paper builds one model in which the small models are contained inside the large one. The first 24 layers form the 500M model, 10 more layers extend it to the 1.5B model, and 5 more layers extend it to the 3B model. Each size has its own output layer (LM head), and all sizes are trained together in a single run. The result is a complete suite from one training run, with fewer parameters in total (3.2B instead of 5.2B).

The idea is hard to see in the paper, because it is spread over three places. The structure (which layers are shared between the sub-models) is in the text of Section 2. The mechanism that connects the sub-models, the junction, appears only in Equation 1. The numbers behind the savings are in Table 1. A new reader has to combine all three to understand why this works and why it is cheaper.

The figure:

How to read it.

  • Left panel: a standard suite. Three independent models, each with its own embedding and LM head, trained in three separate runs. The total is 5.2B parameters.
  • Right panel: a Matryoshka suite. One stack of three blocks (24, +10 and +5 layers). The blue block is exactly the 500M model. Blue plus orange is the 1.5B model. All three blocks together are the 3B model. Each sub-model has its own LM head, so it can be detached and used alone. The total is 3.2B parameters (Table 1 of the paper).
  • Bottom panel: the junction. The output of sub-model m is rescaled to match the norm of the new token embedding, and then it is concatenated with that embedding. The embedding fills the extra channels that the wider sub-model m+1 needs. This adds no new parameters. In the paper’s ablation at 200M scale, removing the rescaling costs about 0.2 validation perplexity, and filling the new channels with zeros costs about 0.54.

The figure shows the parameter count: 3.2B instead of 5.2B (about 38% fewer). The paper’s “36% less training compute” is a separate measurement of training cost, so the two numbers are close but not the same.
entry.summary: One figure that shows how three separate models become one nested model, and where the savings come from.

entry.title: Does sharing KV cache ruin alignment and why do we apply forward KL-Divergence

link.title: Does sharing KV cache ruin alignment and why do we apply forward KL-Divergence

entry.content:
• To Cache or Not to Cache: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Incompatibility in Cross-Model KV Cache Reuse (Lin, Liu, Liu & Wang, 2026): This paper shows that using the KV cache from a base model in its instruct version makes it lose its safety training, meaning it stops refusing harmful requests (Llama-3-8B answers 6% -> 31%). That raises the question: does Matryoshka training keep the safety of the larger model when its sub-models share a KV cache?
  • Divergence controls entropy in distillation (Zucchet & Linderman, 2026): This paper shows that when distilling a student model from a teacher, the choice of forward or reverse KL controls the confidence of the student model: forward KL makes it less confident than the teacher, reverse KL more confident. This might explain the stability of Matryoshka training, since its forward-KL distillation keeps the small models from collapsing onto a live teacher that is still training.
entry.summary: 2 papers similar to parts of the paper

entry.title: Visualizing 🪆 Models
entry.content:
Architecture

The suggested Matryoshka Architecture Suite, outlined in the paper, essentially builds nested sub-models, such that each one is composed of its predecessors:

The Junction Mechanism

To deal with the size mismatch between the different submodels, they suggest the following “Junction” mechanism:

We do 2 things here:

  1. match the norm of the output, to the norm of the next sub-models’ embedding of the input.
  2. concat the normalized output from the previous model, to the input embedding, and feed both to the next submodel.

The Key Idea

The nested structure that we visualized here, is what allows the Matryushka models to be modular - we essentially trained one model (the largest one), and recieved the smaller models “for free” (hence the 36% reduction in training compute). The benefits of the structure are also related to sharing the KV-cache,and allowing for easier inter-model tasks, namely Speculative Decoding and Model Distillation.
entry.summary: Diagrams of the nested model suite and its junction mechanism.
